verdicts.strongest_argument: The finding's own sentence concedes it: 'the split-release structure (revenue in July, full accounts in September) is standard for European issuers'. Standard practice, followed by this issuer at every reporting cycle, is the definition of structural and known - every holder of a European luxury name knows the top line comes first and the margins come with the half-year accounts, and the baseline's median reaction of 1.75% across eight matched events is the market's long-standing acknowledgement of exactly that. The July revenue release is also published and captured: a 6-K dated 2026-07-23 in filings.json and a 'Q2 26 Earnings Results & Recap' entry in the admissible stored body (docs/43f565083d963dd453a2e5a3a2e636882ad642e2.txt, entry 2026-07-23T11:59:21Z), and the baseline records the reaction to it as -0.5%. So the claim that 'the revenue surprise is already in the price' is correct and is the opposite of an edge - it is an argument that this print carries less information than a normal one. What is offered as the unpriced residual, that the whole surprise now sits in gross margin and operating leverage, is a statement about which line to watch, not a view on what that line will say, and it has no size and no sign. The supporting point that 'no consensus anywhere in the capture' anchors a margin expectation is an n_queries=0 artefact; European luxury is among the most heavily covered sectors in the market and a margin consensus certainly exists outside this capture.

The market's own record says releases from this issuer do not move it much - which is the finding's conclusion, already sealed into the baseline.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: A dated pre-print margin datapoint - a peer's wholesale commentary, an input-cost or currency disclosure, a channel inventory reading - that would give the composition argument a direction instead of only a location.

verdicts.strongest_argument: This is a claim built entirely from the baseline's own run-up fields and then read as evidence that something is unpriced, which inverts the logic. run_up_20d of -17.42% and run_up_5d of -8.52% are the market pricing something; calling the move 'unexplained' because this capture holds no company filing after 2026-08-24 and one social message in six weeks is an argument from the absence of evidence in a corpus with no news search at all. The stated principle - 'unexplained moves into a print are more often information than noise' - carries no source and is not testable here. There is also a quantitative problem that I think is decisive. This issuer's eight matched releases have a median absolute reaction of 1.75% and a maximum of 5.30%, against a 17.4% pre-print drift. A name whose price moves ten times more between prints than on them is not one where print information is the driver, so attributing a 17% drift to anticipation of a release that historically moves the stock under two percent is a mismatch of an order of magnitude. The hunter's own alternative - a coincident consumer-discretionary and luxury de-rating, evidenced from the LULU capture in this same run - is both more parsimonious and better supported, and it is why the finding is correctly kept small.
